title: test-0018-SCI-PHY-EYE10
passage: As the sun dips toward the horizon during a late afternoon trek, the sky undergoes a dramatic transformation. Observers often notice the sun appearing slightly higher than its actual position, a phenomenon caused by atmospheric refraction as light bends through layers of varying air density. Simultaneously, the sun takes on a deep reddish hue. This is not because the sun is cooling down, but because the light travels through a thicker layer of the atmosphere, scattering away shorter blue wavelengths and leaving only the longer red wavelengths to reach our eyes. High above, a sudden rain shower creates a brilliant rainbow. Contrary to popular belief, this is not a physical object hanging in the sky, but an optical illusion created by the dispersion, refraction, and reflection of sunlight within tiny water droplets. Meanwhile, a hiker struggling to read a map realizes their eyes are straining. Their ciliary muscles must work harder to change the curvature of the eye lens, making it thicker to focus on nearby text. If the lens cannot adjust sufficiently, the person may require a convex lens to correct this hypermetropia, ensuring light focuses precisely on the retina rather than behind it.
summary: Observers notice the sun appears slightly higher as light bends through layers of air. This is not because the sun is cooling down, but because the light travels through a thicker layer of the atmosphere, so it gets scattered and only leaves the longer red wavelengths to reach our eyes.
